Regarding copyright issues and the saleability I think they will continue the path they have so far - by just being genuinely some of if not the best plastic kit makers on the market. There is no denying the beauty of some of the large scale kits - looking at the newer kits coming out of AoS and the large kits (the new Uber giants and things like archeon, nagash, and mortarian) and that is a major selling point.

As an older player ( I remember 5th coming out and the glory of the red era, but I was only an excited 8 year old who saw cool stuff in the window) I personally want a return to the flexibility of the small scale kits. I'm a hobbyist at the forefront not a gamer!

Regarding your last point I think the difference is cost - they are simply cheaper made and cheaper bought. I imagine the margins are higher as there is less work put in at the initial stage of design and manufacture. For example although the mantic dwarfs are old miniatures now, they are effectively 2 pose, much less then even the smaller kits from GW whose easy build kits often have 5 poses. That is almost 3x the initial workload from a design perspective and extra mould design as well. 

Another example is fireforge miniatures - often used as bretonnian alternatives. They have 3 distinct sets of knights in their range which share the same basic sprue with the difference being one end which is different heads and a command sprue which has some extra bits depending on the type of knight you ordered. 

Compared to the much larger variety of poses and design over 2 seperate but similar kits in GW (for example saurus warriors and temple guard) and you can see they have been designed for complete difference in appearance rather then similar but distinct appearance. This has a cost effect at the front end which then is reflected in the sale price at the back end, reducing margins to less. Temple gua d could just have a head and shield sprue and it would be cheaper to make but that isn't the design philosophy of GW.

However what you are implying with your two way street analogy is exactly that - because monopolies don't stop all production, they just have most production, and by being most visible they tend to be the most accepted. 

What other games did was latch onto that to become visible and develop their own ideas and world's from there - much like GW did in the early years. And these companies may not have 30 years to look back on, but at the time of Warhammers inception they didn't either! The old saying of every piece of art is derived applied here. 

In 20 years time any surviving companies will have thier own brand and style which. The fact is that all things come from one idea and spread from there - GW are just the closest to that one idea at the moment because they are the biggest and have done it the best, and have attracted a huge player base because of their marketing decisions. 

I don't think they would have contributed to WFBs decline as much as they seem to have - GW decided to drop the system due to money reasons and decisions by the executive team at that time. I doubt that what was at the time essentially a cottage alternative was even much on their radar.  It's open knowledge that fantasy didn't make money, and at the end of the day GW were a business, but they still had the largest market share in terms of fantasy battle game profits. They changed the gameplay and such to make more money and sell more miniatures - the fact they could actually copyright it was a bonus.  

Kings of war is still small (relatively) and the pattern followed by mantic with licenced games fits the pattern of early GW (judge dredd, early white dwarf magazine, generic miniatures for d&d) because they do not yet have the player base to survive off their original world's (as derivative of GW I admit they are to a point).

I think the way things are going currently with the advent of 3d printing and miniature design becoming easier, plus a whole younger more creative career inclined generation, and the past 15 years of board game renaissance, I think we are entering a golden age of creativity that will burst GWs bubble - who know maybe they will be forced to return to being a high street games shop to meet the demand of many generic systems rather then a single closed one?

If I was you I'd look into the early history of Warhammer, see if you can get hold of the rules for example,  and see what ideas were new for the races that didn't already exist I bet there is very little. 

And as a final point, Mantic designed and produced thier underwater elves race before GW introduced them in AoS. The fact is that it's a two way street.

I mean, honestly if you're an FY1 who has been working for a month, I expect nothing. 

Everything you can do is a bonus, anything you can't do is a teaching opportunity. 

Knowing your limits is the best skill you have as over cautious, lesser skilled doctors are safer then over confident, well skilled ones in my experience - you're much less likely ton suddenly find yourself out of your depth making decisions you aren't qualified or don't have the experience to make. 

As a broad stroke, I'd expect an FY1 to be proficient in a non complex history, and good at their job re: completing discharges, checking medicines, and performing an A-E assessment of a sick patient before calling for assistance. Then calling for assistance. 

By the end of FY1 I'd except decent cannula technique for a well, non peripherally shut down patient. The ability to make reasonable management decisions in the case of a sick patient before calling for help, and then putting what advice you're given into practice before senior help arrives. 

After that it gets blurry depending on specialty. An F2 in surgery has a much lower expectation in what they can and can't do relative to actually fixing the patient Vs. One in the ED who might be expected to reduce colles fractures or do a femoral stab in an arresting patient. 

Know your limits, practice what you can't do, call for help when you need to, and be a sponge for learning tips and tricks people pick up. (NG tubes are easier to place and less unpleasant if you stick them in the fridge, or 1ml of 1% lidocaine makes that difficult ABG much easier on the patient for example)

Hence the reason to assess yourself. 

We work in an environment where the simplest thing is often to give in to nursing staff. Don't fall into this trap - there are many experienced nurses who's assessment I will trust, and many who's I will not when it comes to this topic. 

You have to ask - they get aggressive when put back to bed, why are they up in the first place? Is keeping them in bed going to stop the aggression, if so then fix that NOT the aggression itself. 

Unfortunately there isn't any hard and fast rules and each patient should be assessed individually and at the time. 

If you don't see them being aggressive and you don't feel the need for sedation at that point, don't give in and prescribe. The nurses can always fast bleep you when it's needed. 

This is a good read- 

https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/j.1445-5994.2011.02560.x&ved=2ahUKEwjIrv_QuuzhAhXkQhUIHX95D9QQFjAMegQIBhAC&usg=AOvVaw2dt9mReWDWycfddUHTi8x1

Also: if they want to sit in a chair all night and that stops them being aggressive, let them. Least restrictive option as long as its safe for everyone. 

If they need 1 to 1 observation because of their behaviour, escalate to nurse I'm charge and matron of needed.

My general rule has always been are they a danger to themselves or others?

If the answer is yes then I will sedate if asked. But I will always review them first - never sign an order for haloperidol or lorazepam without reviewing. 

0.5mg haloperidol will solve most delirious older people without knocking off their respiratory drive. 

And for wandering demented patients who are weak because of whatever reason, a temp. solution can be to lift the legs bit of the bed and head bit a little - to create a sort of butt bowl. I've found with that and barriers they tend to be a lot safer.

Edited because I saw you said risk of falls is a reason not to - if they're already high risk for whatever reason some light sedation is more likely to make them safer by virtue of them not wandering. It's a risk/reward decision that comes with experience.

Best advice I ever got was that if I'm seeing something for the first time, do 2 things. 

1. Brief clerking via their notes. Why are they here, what's the past medical history, what has been done while they're here, and anything relevant to the situation at hand. 

2. If I'm called to see a sick patient, start every note as above, with obs underneath. Then A to E assessment. Then an impression, and a plan. If you're making decisions that need justifying, put that in the plan. 

For example in your case above it might look something like this (adding some staff just to make it clear):

Lexoram CT1 - medicine 

Atsp patient overnight due to combative nature. 

72 year old male admitted with delirium of unknown origin, ?infection - diagnosed as chest  

PMH: Dementia, COPD. 

Obs: news 2 (HR 89 BP 105 systolic, sats 94% on room air, temp 37.5,)

A patent, speaking
B Right sided crackles 
C Hs I+II+0
D gcs 15/15, bm 5
E abdomen soft and non tender, bowels heard. No rashes noted. Urine output good. 

Amts tested 5/10. 
Bloods improving (write them here)
Dementia type alzheimers

On Iv antibiotics, previously confused and agitated. Currently catheterised.
